svg.title: The five EVPN route types, what each one carries, and the job it does in the design
svg.desc: Five rows, one per route type. Type 1 is Ethernet auto-discovery, announcing which ESI a PE owns and used for fast convergence, aliasing and mass withdrawal. Type 2 is the MAC or IP advertisement, the core type that enables ARP proxying and MAC mobility. Type 3 is the inclusive multicast Ethernet tag, which builds the BUM distribution tree. Type 4 is the Ethernet segment route, used for designated forwarder election. Type 5 is the IP prefix route, which lets EVPN carry Layer 3 VPN functions. A memory hook at the bottom reads one discovery, two MAC, three flooding, four election, five prefix, and a note points out that Type 5 is what makes EVPN one control plane for both Layer 2 and Layer 3.
svg.text: Five route types, each one answering a different question in the design
You rarely configure these by name; you do choose them by asking which problem the domain has
NAME
WHAT IT CARRIES
WHAT IT IS FOR IN THE DESIGN
Ethernet A-D
auto-discovery
Announces which ESI this PE owns, and per-EVI state
withdrawn as a batch when the segment goes away
Fast convergence, aliasing load sharing,
and mass withdrawal in one update
MAC / IP advertisement
the core type
A MAC, optionally with its IP, plus the next hop
this is the route that replaces flooding
ARP proxying and MAC mobility;
everything you actually buy EVPN for
Inclusive multicast
IMET, per Ethernet tag
Which PEs want to receive flooded traffic
for this EVI and this tag
Builds the BUM distribution tree,
so floods go where they are wanted
Ethernet segment
per ESI, per PE
Each PE’s view of the same multihomed segment
the input to designated forwarder election
DF election: exactly one PE forwards
BUM towards the multihomed CE
IP prefix
L3 in the same plane
IP prefixes with the usual BGP behaviour
advertised and withdrawn like L3VPN routes
Layer 3VPN functions inside EVPN —
one control plane for L2 and L3
MEMORY HOOK
say it once, then read the table only when the design stalls
Type 5 is the strategic one. It means EVPN can do Layer 2 and Layer 3 at once,
which is the foundation of the single overlay control plane in modern data centres
and campuses — the design thread that returns in Chapter 9
Design reflex: a slow-convergence complaint points to Type 1, a flooding complaint to Types 2 and 3, a duplicate-BUM complaint to Type 4, and a migration complaint to Type 2’s mobility sequence.
